sections.title: Context-free grammars
sections.snippet: A  (CFG) is a set of rules that define how to produce valid text in a given format.

sections.title: Keep grammars simple
sections.snippet: Try to make your grammar as simple as possible.

sections.title: Correct versus incorrect patterns
sections.snippet:
Correct (single, bounded terminal):


start: SENTENCE
SENTENCE: /[A-Za-z, ](the hero|a dragon|an old man|the princess)[A-Za-z, ](fought|saved|found|lost)[A-Za-z, ](a treasure|the kingdom|a secret|his way)[A-Za-z, ]\.

sections.title: Terminals versus rules
sections.snippet: Lark uses terminals for lexer tokens (by convention, UPPERCASE) and rules for parser productions (by convention, lowercase).

sections.title: Key ideas and best practices
sections.snippet:
Lexer runs before the parser

Terminals are matched by the lexer (greedily / longest match wins) before any CFG rule logic is applied.

sections.title: Key ideas and best practices
sections.snippet:
Pattern must be on one line

If you need to match a newline in the input, use the escaped sequence \n.

sections.title: Introduction & Overview
sections.snippet: ROOST and OpenAI have prepared a guide that explains how to write policy prompts that maximize  reasoning power, choose the right policy length for deep analysis, and integrate oss-safeguard's reasoning outputs into production Trust & Safety systems.

sections.title: What is gpt-oss-safeguard?
sections.snippet: gpt-oss-safeguard is a first open weight reasoning model specifically trained for safety classification tasks to help classify text content based on customizable policies.

sections.title: How to Use gpt-oss-safeguard
sections.snippet: Like the , this is an open source model with open weights that you run locally or integrate into your own infrastructure.

- ML/AI Engineers working on Trust & Safety systems who need flexible content moderation
- Trust

sections.title: Writing Effective Policy Prompts for gpt-oss-safeguard
sections.snippet: oss-safeguard performs best when policies are organized like a Trust & Safety policy guide rather than an essay.

sections.title: Understanding Policy Prompting
sections.snippet: A policy prompt defines the operational boundaries of a model’s behavior.

sections.title: Structuring Policy Prompts
sections.snippet: Policy prompts should have four separate sections.

sections.title: INSTRUCTIONS
sections.snippet: Describe what oss-safeguard should do and how to respond.

sections.title: DEFINITIONS
sections.snippet: Clarify key terms and context.

sections.title: VIOLATES (1)
sections.snippet: Describe behaviors or content that should be flagged.

sections.title: SAFE (0)
sections.snippet: Describe content that should not be flagged.

sections.title: EXAMPLES
sections.snippet: Provide 4–6 short examples labeled 0 or 1.

sections.title: Choosing the Right Policy Length
sections.snippet: Policy length is a key control over how deeply gpt-oss-safeguard can reason about your rules.

sections.title: Designing reliable output instructions
sections.snippet: Consistent responses from gpt-oss-safeguard require explicit, literal output instructions.

sections.title: Binary Responses
sections.snippet: Binary output limits gpt-oss-safeguard's reasoning to a simple yes/no decision.

sections.title: Policy-referencing outputs
sections.snippet: Category labels encourage gpt-oss-safeguard to reason about which section of your policy applies, but don't require detailed explanation of why.

sections.title: Including Rationale
sections.snippet: One of the most powerful features of gpt-oss-safeguard is its ability to think and reason.

sections.title: Using gpt-oss-safeguard for Trust & Safety
sections.snippet: Because gpt-oss-safeguard interprets written rules rather than static categories, gpt-oss-safeguard adapts to different product, regulatory, and community contexts with minimal engineering overhead.

sections.title: Automated content classification
sections.snippet: Use gpt-oss-safeguard to label posts, messages, or media metadata for policy violations.

sections.title: T\&S Assistant
sections.snippet: gpt-oss-safeguard's reasoning capabilities make it uniquely suited for automated triage in Trust & Safety workflows.

sections.title: Policy Testing
sections.snippet: Before rolling out a new or revised policy, run it through gpt-oss-safeguard to simulate how content will be labeled.

sections.title: Policy Experimentation
sections.snippet: gpt-oss-safeguard’s bring-your-own-policy design allows policy teams to A/B test alternative definitions directly in production without model retraining.

sections.title: Off-the-shelf Teen Safety Policies
sections.snippet: While safety classifiers like gpt-oss-safeguard can detect harmful content, they depend on clear definitions of what that content is.

sections.title: Example Dangerous Content Policy
sections.snippet: markdown

sections.title: Definitions
sections.snippet: - Dangerous activities or challenges: Activities, stunts, or online challenges that could realistically cause physical injury, poisoning, suffocation, overdose, burns, falls, or other serious harm if attempted by a teenager.

sections.title: Allowed Content (DC0 - Non-dangerous or Safety-oriented)
sections.snippet: Content that discourages risk, provides safety guidance, or discusses challenges critically or educationally without enough detail to mimic.

sections.title: Promotion or Glorification of Dangerous Challenges (DC1 - Promotion)
sections.snippet: Content that celebrates, encourages, or positively frames participation in dangerous activities without giving explicit instructions.

sections.title: Facilitating Dangerous Activities (DC2 - Facilitation or instruction)
sections.snippet: Content that enables or instructs someone to perform dangerous challenges or stunts.

sections.title: Dangerous At-Home Procedures (DC3 - Facilitation or instruction)
sections.snippet: Content that enables or instructs teenagers to perform medical, cosmetic, or body-modification procedures at home without professional supervision.

sections.title: Label Format
sections.snippet: Each item gets one label indicating the presence and type of dangerous content.

sections.title: Ambiguity and Escalation
sections.snippet: - If the user shows clear intent to attempt a dangerous challenge, treat enabling responses as DC2.

sections.title: AI Memory Architecture Decisions
sections.snippet: AI memory is still a new concept, and there is no one-size-fits-all solution.

sections.title: Structured Memory (Schema-driven, machine-enforceable, predictable)
sections.snippet: These should follow strict formats, be validated, and used directly in logic, filtering, or booking APIs.

sections.title: Unstructured Memory (Narrative, contextual, semantic)
sections.snippet: These are freeform and optimized for reasoning, personalization, and human-like decision-making.

sections.title: User-Level Memory (Global Notes)
sections.snippet: Durable preferences that should persist across sessions and influence future interactions.

sections.title: Session-Level Memory (Session Notes)
sections.snippet: Short-lived or contextual information relevant only to the current interaction.

sections.title: 4.1 Memory Distillation
sections.snippet: Memory distillation extracts high-quality, durable signals from the conversation and records them as memory notes.

sections.title: 4.2 Memory Consolidation
sections.snippet: Memory consolidation runs asynchronously at the end of each session, graduating eligible session notes into global memory when appropriate.

sections.title: 4.3 Memory Injection
sections.snippet: Inject curated memory back into the model context at the start of each session.

sections.title: 1.1 Basics
sections.snippet: - Cache hits require an exact, repeated prefix match and works automatically for prompts containing 1024 tokens or more, with cache hits occurring in increments of 128 tokens.

sections.title: 2.1 Core Technical Reason: Skipping Prefill Compute
sections.snippet: The forward pass through transformer layers over the input tokens is the main driver of inference cost and latency.

sections.title: 2.2 Cost Impact
sections.snippet: Cache discounts can be significant.

sections.title: 2.3 Latency Impact
sections.snippet: Reducing time-to-first-token (TTFT) is a primary motivation for improving cache rates.

sections.title: 3.1 Per-request: `cached_tokens`
sections.snippet: Responses include usage fields indicating how many prompt tokens were served from the cache.

sections.title: 4.1 Send a Prompt over 1024 tokens
sections.snippet: It can feel counterintuitive, but in some cases, making your prompt slightly longer can reduce overall cost.

sections.title: 4.2 Stabilize the Prefix
sections.snippet: This is the lowest-effort, highest-impact optimization: keep the early portion of the prompt stable.

sections.title: 4.3 Keep Tools and Schemas Identical
sections.snippet: Tools, schemas, and their ordering contribute to the cached prefix - they get injected before developer instructions which means that changing them would invalidate the cache.

sections.title: Static “tools” stay in the cached prompt prefix:
sections.snippet: tools = [getweatherdef, getlocationdef, calendardef, …]

sections.title: Per-call “allowed_tools” only lives in request metadata, not in the prefix:
sections.snippet: allowedtools = {"mode":"auto", "tools":["getweather","getlocation"]}

sections.title: 4.4 Use `prompt_cache_key` to Improve Routing Stickiness
sections.snippet: Caching only works if two requests share the same prefix and land on the same machine.

sections.title: 4.5 Use the Responses API instead of Chat Completions
sections.snippet: As we outlined in , our internal benchmarks show a 40-80% better cache utilization on requests when compared to Chat Completions.

sections.title: 4.6 Be thoughtful about Context Engineering
sections.snippet: At its core, context engineering is about deciding what goes into the model’s input on each request.

sections.title: 7.1 Retention Ratio
sections.snippet: By default (truncation: "auto"), the server removes just enough old messages to fit within the context window.

sections.title: Conclusion
sections.snippet: Prompt caching is one of the highest-leverage optimizations available on the OpenAI platform.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.snippet: This track is designed for developers and technical learners who want to build production-ready AI applications with OpenAI's models and tools.

This track helps you quickly gain the skills to ship production-ready AI applications in four phases:

1.

- Basic coding familiarity: You should be comfortable with Python or JavaScript.

- Core logic: what your application does, potentially driven by one or several AI agents
- Evaluations (evals): how you measure the qual

sections.title: Evaluations

sections.title: When to use `codex exec`
sections.snippet:
Use codex exec when you want Codex to:

- Run as part of a pipeline (CI, pre-merge checks, scheduled jobs).

sections.title: Basic usage
sections.snippet:
Pass a task prompt as a single argument:

bash
codex exec "summarize the repository structure and list the top 5 risky areas"


While codex exec runs, Codex streams progress to stderr and prints only the final agent message to stdout.

sections.title: Permissions and safety
sections.snippet: By default, codex exec runs in a read-only sandbox.

sections.title: Make output machine-readable
sections.snippet:
To consume Codex output in scripts, use JSON Lines output:

bash
codex exec --json "summarize the repo structure" | jq


When you enable --json, stdout becomes a JSON Lines (JSONL) stream so you can capture every event Codex emits while it's running.

sections.title: Resume a non-interactive session
sections.snippet:
If you need to continue a previous run (for example, a two-stage pipeline), use the resume subcommand:

bash
codex exec "review the change for race conditions"
codex exec resume --last "fix the race conditions you found"


You can also target a specific session ID with codex exec resume <SESSIONID>.

sections.snippet: > For the complete documentation index, see .

sections.title: What is Codex Security?
sections.snippet: Software security remains one of the hardest and most important problems in engineering.

sections.title: Why does it matter?
sections.snippet: Software is foundational to modern industry and society, and vulnerabilities create systemic risk.

sections.title: What business problem does Codex Security solve?
sections.snippet: Codex Security shortens the path from a suspected issue to a confirmed, reproducible finding with evidence and a proposed patch.

sections.title: How does Codex Security work?
sections.snippet: Codex Security runs analysis in an ephemeral, isolated container and temporarily clones the target repository.

sections.title: Does it replace SAST?
sections.snippet: No. Codex Security complements SAST. It adds semantic, LLM-based reasoning and automated validation, while existing SAST tools still provide broad deterministic coverage.

sections.title: What is the analysis pipeline?
sections.snippet:
Codex Security follows a staged pipeline:

1.

sections.title: What languages are supported?
sections.snippet: Codex Security is language-agnostic.

sections.title: What outputs do I get after the scan completes?
sections.snippet: You get ranked findings with criticality, validation status, and a proposed patch when one is available.

sections.title: How is customer code isolated?
sections.snippet: Each analysis and validation job runs in an ephemeral Codex container with session-scoped tools.

sections.title: Does Codex Security auto-apply patches?
sections.snippet: No. The proposed patch is a recommended remediation. Users can review it and push it as a PR to GitHub from the findings UI, but Codex Security does not auto-apply changes to the repository.

sections.title: Does the project need to be built for scanning?
sections.snippet: No. Codex Security can produce findings from repository and commit context without a compile step. During auto-validation, it may try to build the project inside the container if that helps reproduce

sections.title: How does Codex Security reduce false positives and avoid broken patches?
sections.snippet: Codex Security uses two stages.

sections.title: How long do initial scans take, and what happens after that?
sections.snippet: Initial scan time depends on repository size, build time, and how many findings proceed to validation.

sections.title: What is a threat model?
sections.snippet: A threat model is the scan-time security context for a repository.

sections.title: How is a threat model generated?
sections.snippet: Codex Security prompts the model to summarize the repository architecture and security entry points, classify the repository type, run specialized extractors, and merge the results into a project overview or threat model artifact used throughout the scan.

sections.title: Does it replace manual security review?
sections.snippet: No. Codex Security accelerates review and helps rank findings, but it does not replace code-level validation, exploitability checks, or human threat assessment.

sections.title: Can I edit the threat model?
sections.snippet: Yes. Codex Security creates the initial threat model, and you can update it as the architecture, risks, and business context change. For the editing workflow, see .

sections.title: Do I need to configure a scan before using threat modeling?
sections.snippet: Yes. Threat-model guidance is tied to how and what you scan, so you need to configure the repository first. See .

sections.title: What does the proposed patch contain?
sections.snippet: The proposed patch contains a minimal actionable diff with filename and line context when a remediation can be generated for the finding.

sections.title: Does the patch directly modify my PR branch?
sections.snippet: No. The workflow generates a diff, patch file, or suggested change for maintainers and reviewers to inspect before applying.

sections.title: What is auto-validation?
sections.snippet: Auto-validation is the phase that tries to reproduce a suspected issue in an isolated container.

sections.title: What happens if validation fails?
sections.snippet: The finding remains unvalidated.

all_features.feature: Writing Effective Policy Prompts for gpt-oss-safeguard
all_features.snippet: oss-safeguard performs best when policies are organized like a Trust & Safety policy guide rather than an essay.
A policy prompt defines the operational boundaries of a model’s behavior.
Policy prompts should have four separate sections.
Describe what oss-safeguard should do and how to respond.
Clarify key terms and context.
Describe behaviors or content that should be flagged.
Describe content that should not be flagged.
Provide 4–6 short examples labeled 0 or 1.
Policy length is a key control over how deeply gpt-oss-safeguard can reason about your rules.
Consistent responses from gpt-oss-safeguard require explicit, literal output instructions.
Binary output limits gpt-oss-safeguard's reasoning to a simple yes/no decision.
Category labels encourage gpt-oss-safeguard to reason about which section of your policy applies, but don't require detailed explanation of why.
One of the most powerful features of gpt-oss-safeguard is its ability to think and reason.
Because gpt-oss-safeguard interprets written rules rather than static categories, gpt-oss-safeguard adapts to different product, regulatory, and community contexts with minimal engineering overhead.
Use gpt-oss-safeguard to label posts, messages, or media metadata for policy violations.
gpt-oss-safeguard's reasoning capabilities make it uniquely suited for automated triage in Trust & Safety workflows.
Before rolling out a new or revised policy, run it through gpt-oss-safeguard to simulate how content will be labeled.
gpt-oss-safeguard’s bring-your-own-policy design allows policy teams to A/B test alternative definitions directly in production without model retraining.
While safety classifiers like gpt-oss-safeguard can detect harmful content, they depend on clear definitions of what that content is.

Fine-tuning adapts a model to your use case's specific needs, improving its reliability and relevance.
Distillation is a way to transfer a stronger model's behavior to a smaller "student" model, maintaining performance while improving speed and cost.
In this section, we'll cover the practical aspects of fine-tuning, evals, and distillation.

all_features.feature: What business problem does Codex Security solve?
all_features.snippet: Codex Security shortens the path from a suspected issue to a confirmed, reproducible finding with evidence and a proposed patch.
Codex Security runs analysis in an ephemeral, isolated container and temporarily clones the target repository.
No. Codex Security complements SAST. It adds semantic, LLM-based reasoning and automated validation, while existing SAST tools still provide broad deterministic coverage.

Codex Security follows a staged pipeline:

1.
Codex Security is language-agnostic.

all_features.feature: What outputs do I get after the scan completes?
all_features.snippet: You get ranked findings with criticality, validation status, and a proposed patch when one is available.
Each analysis and validation job runs in an ephemeral Codex container with session-scoped tools.
No. The proposed patch is a recommended remediation. Users can review it and push it as a PR to GitHub from the findings UI, but Codex Security does not auto-apply changes to the repository.

all_features.feature: Does the project need to be built for scanning?
all_features.snippet: No. Codex Security can produce findings from repository and commit context without a compile step. During auto-validation, it may try to build the project inside the container if that helps reproduce

all_features.feature: How does Codex Security reduce false positives and avoid broken patches?
all_features.snippet: Codex Security uses two stages.

all_features.feature: How long do initial scans take, and what happens after that?
all_features.snippet: Initial scan time depends on repository size, build time, and how many findings proceed to validation.
A threat model is the scan-time security context for a repository.

all_features.feature: How is a threat model generated?
all_features.snippet: Codex Security prompts the model to summarize the repository architecture and security entry points, classify the repository type, run specialized extractors, and merge the results into a project overview or threat model artifact used throughout the scan.

all_features.feature: Does it replace manual security review?
all_features.snippet: No. Codex Security accelerates review and helps rank findings, but it does not replace code-level validation, exploitability checks, or human threat assessment.

all_features.feature: Can I edit the threat model?
all_features.snippet: Yes. Codex Security creates the initial threat model, and you can update it as the architecture, risks, and business context change. For the editing workflow, see .

all_features.feature: Do I need to configure a scan before using threat modeling?
all_features.snippet: Yes. Threat-model guidance is tied to how and what you scan, so you need to configure the repository first. See .

all_features.feature: What does the proposed patch contain?
all_features.snippet: The proposed patch contains a minimal actionable diff with filename and line context when a remediation can be generated for the finding.

all_features.feature: Does the patch directly modify my PR branch?
all_features.snippet: No. The workflow generates a diff, patch file, or suggested change for maintainers and reviewers to inspect before applying.
Auto-validation is the phase that tries to reproduce a suspected issue in an isolated container.
The finding remains unvalidated.

When you run Codex natively on Windows, agent mode uses a Windows sandbox to

without your explicit approval.

Running Codex in full access mode means Codex is not limited to your project

text

sandbox mode, Windows version, and any policy error shown by Codex.
